title: Dynamic Nuclear Polarization MR Spectroscopic Imaging for Diagnosis and Treatment Response Assessment in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
text:
The diagnosis of HCC and assessment of its response to treatment rely primarily on imaging
biomarkers which have replaced tissue-based measures. Recent studies demonstrate significant
limitations of standard-of-care imaging paradigms for: (i) distinguishing HCCs from other tumors
commonly observed in the liver, (ii) informing on the molecular and cellular biology required to
facilitate treatment stratification and (iii) assessing treatment response. The development of the
functional imaging strategies required to address these deficiencies has been limited by the
absence of methodologies that can tailor imaging probe selection to the relevant HCC biology as
well as a dearth of representative animal models. Using genome editing and metabolomics, our
laboratory has demonstrated fundamental enzymatic dependencies of HCC cells to be promising
imaging targets for diagnosis and treatment response assessment using Dynamic Nuclear
Polarization 13Carbon Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopic Imaging, a novel and emerging
imaging technology. The proposed project will build on this prior work to assess the accuracy of
this technology for diagnosing and characterizing HCC and for treatment response assessment
using unique translational animal models developed in our laboratory.

title: Precision targeting of bladder cancer using CRISPR
text:
The goal of this R01 proposal is to assess the efficacy of a new precision cancer targeting
approach using CRISPR technology that brings together a “split” endonuclease precisely at
structural variant junctions in bladder cancer cells. This approach is targeting only the cancer
cells and is not dependent on the specific tumor biology of the cancer. This personalized and
tumor-specific targeting approach is a paradigm-shifting platform technology that could
transform bladder cancer treatments.

title: Paracrine signaling from keratinocytes establishes a pro-melanoma environment
text:
In the normal epidermis, ultraviolet radiation exposure induces the protective tanning response which transiently
upregulates keratinocyte to melanocyte crosstalk. Melanoma cells hijack the protective tanning response,
forcing keratinocytes to release factors that enrich for or stimulate the emergence of stem-like properties in
melanoma cells. This project will investigate the mechanism by which melanoma cells activate pro-
melanomagenic signaling in keratinocytes and the extent to which that signaling enhances melanoma migration,
invasion and drug resistance.

title: Core K: Translational Virology
text: Core K: Translational Virology (TV) Project Summary/Abstract New virological technologies have revolutionalized the understanding of HIV transmission, persistence, and pathogenesis. The overall objective of the Translational Virology (TV) Core is to provide SD CFAR researchers with virologic expertise and advanced laboratory techniques tailored to HIV research. The TV Core will maximize access to specialized assays, develop data processing tools, ensure the highest quality results, and provide excellent training for the next generation of HIV researchers. HIV research efforts require reliable links and smooth communication between clinical and basic science investigators. The TV Core of the SD CFAR has been created, developed, and improved to achieve these objectives. The enhanced SD CFAR TV Core will provide services through four defined units that work closely with other SD CFAR cores, as outlined through our specific aims: 1. Assay Unit: To provide virologic expertise and a diverse array of specialized virologic assays based on the research needs of SD CFAR investigators. 2. Data Processing Unit: To provide computational expertise in the implementation of new data processing pipelines for virologic data, in concert with the Biostatistics and Modeling Core. 3. Training Unit: To provide training in virologic procedures and assist in the development of the next generation of HIV researchers, particularly those from underrepresented backgrounds. 4. Quality Assurance Unit: To ensure the quality, standardization, and integrity of our services. The Core’s restructuring for the upcoming renewal illustrates our commitment to providing the best science and services to all our collaborators. The Core’s four pillars of expertise, innovation, collaboration, and mentoring provide exemplary laboratory support services for all researchers and projects. Specific to this renewal, the proposed new and expanded TV Core will maximize efficiency and eliminate overlap by offering all virologic expertises and technologies ‘under one roof’. This new organization is designed to be the most reliable and cost- effective link that provides added value to HIV research within our Center while strengthening the collaboration and communication with the other SD CFAR cores. The expanded TV Core will bring our Center’s basic and clinical science researchers together and connects them with other SD CFAR cores to achieve the following key objectives: 1) Providing HIV-specific Expertise, 2) Lowering the Cost Barrier to Virologic Research, 3) Supporting Data Processing Pipelines through the new Data Processing Unit, and 4) Training the New Generation of HIV Researchers.

title: Cellular Basis for Autonomic Regulation of Cardiac Arrhythmias
text: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT - Project 2 Sudden cardiac death (SCD) describes the abrupt onset of ventricular arrhythmias that kills more Americans than any other disease. These life-threatening changes in electrical activity are most often observed in people who have suffered a prior myocardial infarction (MI). Unfortunately, our ability to prevent SCD is limited by an incomplete understanding of what actually triggers the underlying arrhythmias. The surviving tissue surrounding the infarcted area of the heart, known as the border zone, is the primary sight of reentrant electrical activity that sustains these events. Electrical heterogeneities in myocytes found in the border zone and more remote areas of the myocardium create a substrate for reentry. However, the generation of arrhythmias associated with SCD is also linked to an increase in sympathetic tone and a decrease in parasympathetic tone. In fact, chronic vagal nerve stimulation (cVNS) has been shown to reduce the incidence of ventricular arrhythmias following an MI. Yet, it is not known how myocytes found in different areas of the infarcted heart respond to autonomic neurotransmitters such as norepinephrine (NE) and acetylcholine (ACh). Furthermore, there is evidence the incidence of arrhythmias is also affected by the release of co-transmitters such as neuropeptide Y (NPY) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). Our working hypothesis is that the sympathetic neurotransmitters NE and NPY, as well as the parasympathetic neurotransmitters ACh and VIP, alter the arrhythmogenic potential of the infarcted heart by regulating electrical heterogeneity as well as triggered activity in different areas. In this Project, we will address the following questions: 1) how do NPY and VIP affect the electrical properties of ventricular myocytes, 2) do sympathetic and parasympathetic neurotransmitters affect electrical heterogeneity and triggered activity of myocytes in the border zone and remote areas of the infarcted heart differently, and 3) does cVNS reduce arrhythmogenesis by remodeling the electrical and pharmacological properties of myocytes in the infarcted heart. A combination of single cell electrophysiology, molecular biology, immunocytochemistry, and biochemical techniques will be used to answer these questions. Changes occurring at the cellular level identified in this Project will be integrated with information about changes in the distribution and function of autonomic nerves observed at the whole heart level in Projects 2 and 3 of this Program Project by using a computational modeling approach to investigate the mechanistic basis for autonomic regulation of arrhythmias. The results of this project will provide the foundation from which the efficacy of targeted neuromodulation can be mechanistically assessed, leading to improved therapeutic strategies for preventing SCD.

title: Center for Advanced Imaging Innovation and Research (CAI2R)
text:
Overall Project Narrative
 The Center for Advanced Imaging Innovation and Research (CAI2R) develops novel imaging techniques and
technologies for the improved diagnosis and management of cancer, musculoskeletal disease, neurological
disease and other disorders with a profound impact on human health. Leveraging novel magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) and sensor hardware, together with rigorous biophysical modeling and artificial intelligence, we
aim to expand biomedical knowledge and improve the care of patients.

title: Socioeconomic Mediators of Adult Brain Network Resilience and Vulnerability to Cognitive Decline
text:
Stress and lifestyle are hypothesized to impact brain and cognitive health over the lifespan, although detailed
examinations of the interplay between these factors during middle-age adulthood are lacking. Our longitudinal
project of midlife brain aging involves deep phenotyping of brain, cognition, stress, lifestyle, and life course
exposures in middle-aged adult individuals who are at higher risk of cognitive decline and brain disease. Our
project will integrate these measures with blood-based biomarkers of Alzheimer’s Disease-related pathology
and neural damage to gain a deeper understanding of the sources of cognitive vulnerability and resilience, in
advance of cognitive impairment and brain disease.

title: Chemistry and Cancer Program
text: The Chemistry and Cancer (CC) Program of the Simmons Comprehensive Cancer Center (SCCC) plays a pivotal role in translating basic science research into groundbreaking cancer therapies. By seamlessly integrating fundamental research with drug discovery, the CC Program has facilitated numerous collaborations, resulting in significant advances in cancer biology and clinically relevant treatment advances. Combining the expertise of synthetic and medicinal chemists, molecular and structural biologists, biomedical engineers, chemical biologists, pharmacologists, and clinician scientists, members of the CC Program are dedicated to discovering, designing, and optimizing small molecules and other therapeutic approaches that target deregulated biological pathways in cancer. The program operates on the premise that interdisciplinary chemistry- and engineering-focused approaches to cancer biology can unlock new avenues for cancer prevention and treatment. The CC Program comprises 27 members from nine departments at UT Southwestern. The central themes of the program are guided by three specific aims: (1) Identification of Molecular Targets of Novel Anti-Cancer Agents, (2) Structure- Based Drug Design of Chemicals that Perturb Cancer-Relevant Signaling Pathways, and (3) Development of Biomedical Engineering Approaches for Cancer Detection, Imaging, and Treatment. Emphasizing the translation of chemical discoveries to the clinic, the CC Program accelerates early-stage translational studies and supports the licensing of mid- to late-stage preclinical studies. The program prioritizes research on cancers prevalent in the SCCC catchment area, including lung, breast, kidney, and liver cancers, and fosters both intra- and inter- programmatic collaborations to explore new projects within its specific aims. SCCC has significantly enhanced the CC program by investing in faculty recruitment, especially in the area of biomedical engineering, providing discretionary and pilot funds to support its missions, and expanding shared resources including the High Throughput Screening Shared Resource (HTSSR). Total direct peer-reviewed funding to the CC Program is $7.9M, with $4.8M (61%) from the NCI. Total direct cancer focused funding is $11M. This represents an increase of 77% since the 2020 competing renewal application. Since 2020, program members have published 210 peer- reviewed articles, with 14% intra-programmatic and 37% inter-programmatic papers. Notably, 37% are published in high-impact journals. By harnessing the power of chemistry and basic science, the CC Program continues to drive innovation in cancer treatment, translating laboratory discoveries into impactful clinical applications. Further, CC members mentor and train young faculty and students across the educational continuum. In addition, the program co-leaders organize regular activities and foster collaborations among members, with an emphasis on the community and catchment area. Strong support from SCCC includes a pilot award program designed to support promising high risk – high reward projects.

title: Elucidating the antiviral mechanisms of OAS family innate immune sensors.
text:
Viral infections continue to pose major threats to public health, and our innate immune system
plays an integral role in detection and early control of these pathogens. The OAS-RNase L innate
immune pathway provides a key defense against many viral infections, however the mechanisms by
which the OAS family proteins interface with virus to initiate diverse antiviral responses remains
unclear. The proposed experiments will define the molecular mechanisms, RNA substrates, and
interactomes of OAS innate immune sensors which may lead to the development of new therapeutics
for combating viral infections and inhibiting disease.

title: Hijacking the neonatal Fc receptor: the novel biology of arterivirus entry, transmission, and persistence
text:
Understanding novel mechanisms by which mammalian viruses enter cells, evade immunity, and cause
disease has scientific and public health importance. In this project, we will unpack the novel biology of a
neglected family of understudied RNA viruses that are distant relatives of coronaviruses, the arteriviruses.
Focusing on interactions between arteriviruses and the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn), we will discover how
arteriviruses hijack this host molecule to gain entry into cells, damage the immune system of their host, and
transmit across the placental barrier to infect the fetus in utero.

title: Investigating the role of TWIST1 during smooth muscle cell phenotypic modulation
text:
This research addresses coronary artery disease, a leading cause of death and disability, by uncovering how
specific smooth muscle cell populations drive plaque growth and instability. By mapping clonal smooth muscle
cell fate and defining how the human risk gene TWIST1 controls their behavior, this project will provide
fundamental insight into the cellular and molecular mechanisms of atherosclerosis. In the long term, these
discoveries may enable the development of targeted therapies that selectively block harmful cell states,
improving cardiovascular outcomes and reducing the burden of heart disease.

title: Environmental ethoxylated surfactants and metabolic health dysregulation in zebrafish
text:
The prevalence of metabolic disorders, such as obesity, continues to increase and impose significant costs on
the US health care system; nearly 20% of children and adolescents and >40% of US adults are obese, and
obesity-related health care costs account for nearly 10% of all US healthcare spending. Exposure to
environmental contaminants has been implicated as a causal factor, and some of these contaminants, termed
metabolic disrupting chemicals (MDCs), increase weight and lipid accumulation and/or perturb energy balance
and/or metabolic homeostasis, contributing to metabolic dysfunction including obesity. This proposed award
will support investigation into causal mechanisms underpinning metabolic health outcomes induced by
exposure to ubiquitous indoor contaminants (polyethoxylated surfactants), supporting a comprehensive
understanding of chemical-induced metabolic dysfunction.

title: Regulation and impact of alternative splicing in biology and disease
text:
Alternative pre-mRNA splicing is a crucial component of establishing appropriate gene expression
programs that are unique to tissues and differentiated cell types. Defects in alternative splicing are
known to associate with many human diseases. In this project we will analyze the mechanisms of
regulated alternative splicing using a combination of experimental and computational approaches to
provide detailed molecular insights into the control of gene expression and to identify novel disease
targets.

title: Molecular Genetic Mechanisms of Infantile Epilepsies and the Impact of Genetic Diagnosis
text:
Infantile epilepsies are common, affecting 1 in 1000 infants, and are associated with significant morbidity,
mortality, healthcare costs, and caregiver burden. Although most infantile epilepsies are believed to have
genetic causes, most infants with epilepsy remain genetically “unsolved” and the full genetic landscape of
infantile epilepsies is unknown, which limits our ability to develop precision therapies and ultimately improve
outcomes for this vulnerable population. This proposal aims to discover new genetic causes of infantile
epilepsies and evaluate the impact of these discoveries on infants with epilepsy and their families, contributing
to knowledge that will inform our scientific understanding of normal and abnormal brain development and guide
clinical care and implementation of precision medicine for infants with epilepsy.

title: Identifying multi-omic signatures of opioid use and relapse
text:
The Opioid Epidemic constitutes a major public health crisis as rates of opioid use and overdose continue to
rise in the United States. Many individuals with opioid user disorder struggle to remain abstinent, even those
who have undergone treatment, necessitating development of new therapeutics. We will deepen our
understanding of how opioid use changes the brain to promote relapse by identifying and manipulating activity-
dependent transcriptional and epigenetic changes in an opioid self-administration mouse model, thereby
informing new treatment approaches.

title: Characterization of disulfide modified diabetogenic neoepitopes
text:
Autoimmune T cell responses specific to neoepitopes formed in peripheral tissues may explain how and why T
cell responses break the usual tolerance mechanisms. This project investigates how disulfide modified antigens
elicit autoimmune T cell responses and how redox regulation may impact disulfide modified antigen presentation.
The study could provide novel therapeutic strategies to prevent or treat type 1 diabetes.

title: A meta-transcriptomic assessment of chronic respiratory exposure to cobalt-based nanomaterials using a microfluidic three-dimensional lung model for determining potential predisposition to lung injury
text:
Metallic nanomaterials, including cobalt-based, are being designed and used for many
biomedical applications. It is important to fully understand the fate and potential harm of
these materials prior to use in the body, and for the safety of the fabrication scientists.
This proposed study will greater help to understand the potential implications following
chronic inhalation exposure to cobalt or cobalt-oxide nanoparticles.

title: Artificial Intelligence to Predict Outcomes in Patients with Acute Kidney Injury on Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy
text:
Continuous renal replacement therapy is the preferred dialysis treatment for critically ill patients with acute kidney
injury, yet mortality is high. Presently, there are no accurate approaches for predicting survival or kidney recovery
in these patients. We propose to deliver innovative deep learning approaches to predict these outcomes at
actionable timepoints, and identify patient sub-phenotypes for model interpretation and clinical utility testing.

title: Center for Advanced Genome Engineering (CAGE)
text: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT – CENTER FOR ADVANCED GENOME ENGINEERING The Center for Advanced Genome Engineering (CAGE) provides expertise, education, and services supporting established and emerging genome-engineering technologies. The CAGE was established in 2017 based on St. Jude Comprehensive Cancer Center (SJCCC) member feedback and was proposed as a Developing Shared Resource (SR) in the prior grant renewal. The CAGE is directed by Shondra Pruett-Miller, PhDCBP, who has over 20 years of genome-editing experience and is supported by 15 full-time, highly experienced, and multidisciplinary staff members. At its launch, the CAGE offered four services: (1) genome editing reagent design, assembly, and validation; (2) custom-edited clonal cell line creation; (3) targeted deep sequencing and analysis of CRISPR- editing outcomes; and (4) CRISPR-edited rodent model creation in collaboration with the Genetically Engineered Mouse Models SR. In response to member feedback, the CAGE added three services during the project period: (1) genome-edited cell pools, (2) pooled CRISPR screening services, and (3) cellular fitness assays to validate hits from pooled CRISPR screens. Additionally, the CAGE provides expert one-on-one consultations to discuss project objectives and strategies as well as seminars and other presentations on genome editing techniques and CAGE services across campus. Due to high member demand for and satisfaction with CAGE services during the project period, the CAGE team expanded from eight to 16 employees. Additionally, space allocations increased by 912 sq ft, resulting in a current total footprint of 2,258 sq ft. To improve efficiency and increase capacity, the CAGE added several key pieces of equipment, including two Tecan Freedom Evo liquid handling robots, two Multidrop Combi microplate reagent dispensers, a 96-well benchtop pipettor, four additional tissue culture hoods (bringing the total to nine), and six additional incubators (bringing the total to 15). During the reference year (FY2024), the CAGE provided services to 86 investigators at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital. Of these, 61 (71%) were SJCCC members from four of the five research Programs, contributing to 60% of the CAGE chargebacks. Since being included in the annual SR survey, the CAGE has consistently ranked as one of the top SRs in terms of satisfaction, with 97% of members rating their experience as satisfied or strongly satisfied on the 2024 survey. Additionally, during the project period, the CAGE accomplished the creation of over 1, 000 custom-edited clonal cell lines, more than 400 edited cell pools, over 300 cellular-fitness assays, and more than 300 CRISPR-modified rodent models. Over 200 pooled CRISPR screens were also facilitated by the CAGE. The CAGE has had a significant impact, as evidenced by 131 publications from SJCCC members utilizing CAGE services during the current project period. Of these, 78 (59%) were published in high-impact journals (impact factor >10), and 73 (56%) included CAGE personnel as authors.

title: Consolidation and interference of hippocampal spatial maps
text:
Our research indicates neurons in the brain, particularly within the hippocampus, remain active during sleep,
replaying patterns that correspond to previous experiences and contributing to the long-term retention of
memories. We aim to advance our machine learning tools to dissect how these sleep patterns, known as
sharp-wave ripples, contribute to stabilizing memories within different contexts and study the mechanistic role
they play when memory interference occurs. Through a series of experiments, we will analyze the encoding of
experiences by neuronal ensembles during sleep, investigate how sharp-wave ripples aid in segregating
contextual memories, and test if these patterns are crucial for recalling context-specific information, ultimately
enhancing our understanding of memory function.
